pages.x: Lebanon shared power between its religious communities: by custom the president was a Maronite Christian, the prime minister a Sunni Muslim and the speaker a Shia. But Muslims were by then thought to outnumber Christians, and from 1970 the PLO, the Palestinian guerrilla movement, driven from Jordan, made Lebanon its base for attacks on Israel.

On 13 April 1975, after gunmen fired on a church in a Christian suburb of Beirut, Phalangist militiamen ambushed a bus carrying Palestinians and killed about two dozen people. Fighting spread across the city, which was split by the Green Line, named for the weeds that grew along it, into a Christian east and a Muslim west.

The war became a cycle of revenge. Palestinian and leftist fighters massacred the people of the Christian town of Damour; Christian militias besieged and overran the Palestinian camp of Tel al-Zaatar. Gunmen at checkpoints killed people for the religion on their identity cards.

In 1976 Syria's president, Hafez al-Assad, sent his army into Lebanon, at first to stop the Palestinians and their allies from winning. Syrian troops stayed for almost thirty years, and Assad became the most powerful man in Lebanese politics.

In June 1982, after years of PLO raids and Israeli strikes, Israel invaded, drove up the coast and besieged West Beirut for ten weeks. The PLO agreed to leave, and Yasser Arafat sailed into exile in Tunisia. Bashir Gemayel, a Christian leader allied with Israel, was elected president, and was killed by a bomb three weeks later.

Days later Lebanese Christian militiamen entered the Palestinian camps of Sabra and Shatila, in an area guarded by the Israeli army, and over two days killed hundreds of civilians, perhaps many more. An Israeli inquiry found that the defence minister, Ariel Sharon, bore personal responsibility for not preventing it.

American, French and Italian troops came to keep the peace. On 23 October 1983 suicide bombers drove trucks packed with explosives into the barracks of the US Marines and the French paratroopers in Beirut. The peacekeepers left within months.

The war broke into ever smaller wars: Christians against Christians, Shia militias against Palestinians, Druze against Christians in the mountains. A new Shia movement backed by Iran, Hezbollah, fought the Israeli army in the south, and groups linked to it held Western hostages in Beirut, some for years.

In 1989 Lebanon's members of parliament met at Taif in Saudi Arabia, and agreed to share power more evenly between Christians and Muslims. General Michel Aoun, who led one of two rival governments, refused, until Syrian forces defeated him in October 1990. The war was over.

Some 150,000 people were killed, and about a million left the country. The militia leaders were pardoned, and many became politicians; Syria kept its grip on Lebanon until 2005. Beirut was rebuilt, but about 17,000 people who disappeared in the war have never been found.
pts: The Taif Agreement shared power more evenly
